title: Constitutional Amendment 1: Governor Veto Messages and End of the Pocket Veto

context.text: Referred to voters by the New Mexico Legislature as a proposed constitutional amendment; the Secretary of State lists it among four amendments on the November 3, 2026 ballot. A majority of the votes cast on the question is needed to adopt it.

question.text: Proposing an amendment to Article 4, Section 22 of the Constitution of New Mexico to require the governor to provide veto messages on all bills vetoed in whole or in part and to provide that all bills passed by the legislature and not acted on by the governor will become law.

summary.text: Ends the "pocket veto": currently, a bill presented to the governor in the last three days of a session does not become law unless the governor signs it. Under the amendment, such a bill becomes law unless the governor vetoes it within 20 days after adjournment, and every veto (in whole or part) must include an explanation. The guide describes it as requiring a written, substantive explanation for the veto. The legislature passed it in 2025 (House Joint Resolution 2). No fiscal impact is stated in the guide.

measure.yesMeans: Eliminates the pocket veto so that bills not acted on by the governor become law, and requires the governor to give an explanation for every veto.
measure.noMeans: Leaves the constitution unchanged: a bill presented to the governor in the last three days of a session that the governor does not sign does not become law, and no veto explanation is required.

argumentsFor.text: Voter guide argument for: "Provides greater transparency to the public and the legislature regarding why a governor vetoed a bill."
Voter guide argument for: "Potentially brings greater balance among the branches of government."

argumentsAgainst.text: Voter guide argument against: "This proposed amendment is unnecessary and could be overly burdensome." It notes the legislature can already require a veto reason by presenting bills before the last three days of a session.
Voter guide argument against: "The requirement to provide a 'substantive explanation' is undefined," which it says could lead to litigation between the legislative and executive branches.

sources.title: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Constitutional Amendments and General Obligation Bonds

researchNotes: Source: the New Mexico Secretary of State's 2026 Voter Guide and its published ballot question text. The guide reproduces purpose statements and arguments for and against prepared by the legislature (it links nmlegis.gov's Constitutional Amendments 2026 publication) and states that this analysis does not necessarily reflect the Secretary of State's views; arguments are the guide's unattributed summaries, not statements by named campaigns. The Secretary of State says only the title (in capital letters on the joint resolution) appears on the ballot. Required vote: a simple majority. Legislative vote tallies were not retrieved. The Santa Fe County Clerk's 2026 list words this title in a different order (provision on bills becoming law first, then veto messages); the text used here is the Secretary of State's.
